newsitem.title: FRANCE: Britain to rejoin U.N. body following reform drive.
newsitem.headline: Britain to rejoin U.N. body following reform drive.

text.p: The new Labour government is to bring Britain back into UNESCO which it left 12 years ago, complaining of mismanagement and a Third Word slant, new British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook said on Tuesday.

Cook, whose party ended 18 years of rule by the Conservative party this month, told reporters he had confirmed to fellow European foreign ministers that Britain would rejoin UNESCO -- the U.N.'s Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation.

"This is part of our strategy of ending the isolation of Britain in international affairs... Britain intends to play a full part as an active member in the European family of nations," he told a news conference.
Cook was attending a meeting of the Western European Union (WEU) defence body gathering foreign and defence ministers from 28 European countries at UNESCO's Paris headquarters.
He said a formal announcement of the move would be made shortly in London by the minister for international development.

The United States and Britain, two major contributors to UNESCO, left the organisation in 1985, complaining of wasted resources and excessive politicisation under the directorship of Amadou Mahtar M'Bow.
They also opposed attempts to create a new world information order boosting the role of government-controlled news media.
Spain's Federico Mayor took over from M'Bow two years later, carrying out a reorganisation to make it more efficient.
British diplomats said that radical reforms had been made in the running of UNESCO, and it was now carrying out important work in which Britain wanted to be involved.
Washington has indicated it is considering rejoining UNESCO, but a spokeswoman for the organisation said no concrete step had been taken, partly because of U.S. budget problems.
The U.S. needs to pay $65 million a year to regain full membership.
